learn.hook: Indian software runs banks in London, Gulf oil fuels Indian cars, and Japanese technology makes Indian metro coaches. No country is an island in business.
points: International business refers to manufacturing and trade beyond national boundaries. It includes not only cross-border trade in goods and services, but also the movement of capital, personnel, technology and intellectual property (patents, trademarks, know-how and copyrights).

International trade means exports and imports of goods and services. International business is wider: it covers trade plus foreign investment, licensing, franchising and other forms of cross-border operations.

Main reason: countries cannot produce everything equally well or cheaply, because of unequal distribution of natural resources (e.g. oil in the Gulf, iron ore in some countries) and differences in labour productivity and production costs.
So each country specialises in what it can produce more efficiently and trades for the rest. This specialisation benefits all trading nations.

example.q: India imports crude oil but exports IT services. Explain why, using the reasons for international business.
steps: India does not have enough crude oil reserves: unequal distribution of natural resources.
India has a large pool of skilled, cost-effective IT professionals: differences in labour productivity and costs.
So India specialises in IT services and trades for oil.
example.answer: Due to unequal natural resources and differences in labour productivity and costs, India specialises in IT and imports oil.

learn.reallife: Indian generic medicines are exported to many countries because India can produce them at lower cost: specialisation in action.

topics.title: Domestic vs international business; scope of international business

learn.hook: Selling sarees in Jaipur and selling sarees in Japan both involve sarees, but the currency, laws, customers and risks are completely different.
points: Differences between domestic and international business: nationality of buyers and sellers (same vs different countries); nationality of other stakeholders (employees, suppliers, investors); mobility of factors of production (free within a country, restricted across countries); customer heterogeneity (different tastes, languages, cultures); differences in business systems and practices; political systems and risks; business regulations and policies (tariffs, quotas, standards); currency (one currency vs different currencies and exchange-rate changes).

Scope: merchandise exports and imports (tangible goods); service exports and imports, also called invisible trade (tourism and travel, transportation, business services such as banking, insurance, software).
Licensing and franchising: permitting a firm in another country to use patents, trademarks, technical know-how or a business model in return for a fee (royalty).

Foreign investment: foreign direct investment (FDI) means investing directly in plants, machinery or a controlling stake abroad, with control over management; portfolio investment means buying shares or giving loans abroad to earn dividends or interest, without control.

example.q: A US fund buys 2% shares of an Indian listed company only to earn dividends, while a Korean carmaker builds and runs a factory in Tamil Nadu. Classify both investments.
steps: Buying a small stake for dividends, without control = portfolio investment.
Building and running a factory with management control = FDI.
example.answer: US fund: portfolio investment; Korean carmaker: FDI.

learn.hook: When an Indian pharma company sells medicines in Africa, India earns dollars, the company earns more profit, and workers in its plants get more jobs. Everyone wins.
points: Benefits to nations: earning foreign exchange, which helps pay for imports of capital goods, technology and oil.

More efficient use of resources (each country produces what it is good at); improving growth prospects and employment potential; increased standard of living through access to a wider variety of goods and services.
Benefits to firms: prospects for higher profits (when prices abroad are higher); increased capacity utilisation (using surplus capacity by selling abroad).
Prospects for growth (when domestic demand is saturated); a way out of intense competition in the domestic market; improved business vision (thinking globally makes firms more competitive).

topics.title: Modes of entry: exporting/importing and contract manufacturing

learn.hook: A firm can enter a foreign market by just shipping goods there, or by getting a local factory to make its products. These are the two simplest doors to global business.
points: Exporting means sending goods and services from the home country to a foreign country; importing means buying them from abroad. Direct exporting/importing: the firm itself approaches overseas buyers or suppliers and handles all formalities. Indirect: the firm works through intermediaries such as export houses or buying offices of foreign customers.
Merits of exporting/importing: the easiest way to enter international markets; less involvement and less investment (no need to set up units abroad); less risk compared with other modes.

Limitations: added costs of packaging, transportation and insurance make goods costlier abroad; not possible where the importing country has restrictions; exporters operate from home and have little direct contact with foreign markets.

Contract manufacturing (outsourcing): a firm enters into a contract with local manufacturers in foreign countries to produce certain components or goods as per its specifications. Merits: large-scale production without investing in facilities; little investment risk; cost advantage (local labour and materials); local producers get business.

Limitations of contract manufacturing: local firms may not follow quality standards; the local manufacturer loses control over the manufacturing process, since goods are made strictly as per the contract; the local firm cannot sell the goods freely and must sell to the international firm at predetermined prices.

example.q: A European clothing brand gets an Indian factory in Tiruppur to make T-shirts with its designs and labels, and buys all of them at an agreed price. Which mode of entry is this, and one limitation for the Indian factory?
steps: Production by a local firm as per the foreign firm's specifications = contract manufacturing.
The Indian factory must sell to the brand at predetermined prices and cannot sell the T-shirts freely.
example.answer: Contract manufacturing; the local firm cannot sell freely and gets predetermined prices.

learn.reallife: Many global brands get their garments, phones and toys made by contract manufacturers in India.

topics.title: Modes of entry: licensing, franchising, joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries

learn.hook: A burger chain's outlet in Delhi, a car plant owned jointly by Indian and foreign firms, and a foreign company's 100%-owned Indian unit: three deeper ways to go global.
points: Licensing: a firm (licensor) permits a foreign firm (licensee) to use its patents, trademarks, copyrights or technical know-how for a fee called royalty. Franchising is similar but is generally used for services; the franchiser gives a business model and exercises stricter control over the franchisee. Merits: less expensive and low risk for the licensor (licensee invests); licensor does not bear losses; low risk of government takeover as local owners run the business; licensee's local knowledge helps. Limitations: licensee may later become a competitor; trade secrets may leak; conflicts over accounts, royalty and quality.

Joint venture (JV): a firm jointly owned by two or more independent firms. It can be formed when a foreign firm buys an interest in a local firm, a local firm buys an interest in a foreign firm, or both jointly form a new enterprise. Merits: less financial burden for the foreign firm; large projects become possible; benefit of the local partner's knowledge of markets, culture and politics; risks are shared. Limitations: technology and trade secrets may be revealed to the partner; dual ownership can cause conflicts.

Wholly owned subsidiary (WOS): the parent company acquires full control (100% equity) over a foreign company, either by setting up a new firm (greenfield venture) or by acquiring an established firm. Merits: full control over operations; no need to share technology or trade secrets. Limitations: 100% investment, so not suitable for small and medium firms; the parent bears all losses; some countries are averse to full foreign ownership, raising political risk.
Comparing modes: exporting and licensing need the least investment abroad; a joint venture needs more; a wholly owned subsidiary needs the most investment and gives the most control.

example.q: A foreign pizza brand lets an Indian company run outlets under its name, menu and systems, and checks quality strictly in return for fees. Which mode is this, and how does it differ from licensing?
steps: Use of brand plus a full business system in services, with strict control = franchising.
Licensing is mainly for production and marketing of goods using patents or know-how, with less control.
Franchising is mainly for services, with stricter control by the franchiser.
example.answer: Franchising; it applies to services with stricter control, while licensing applies to goods.

learn.reallife: Many international fast-food and coffee chains operate in India through franchise partners, while some automobile companies run 100% subsidiaries.

topics.title: Export procedure (I): from enquiry to production

learn.hook: A buyer in Dubai emails an Indian carpet maker in Bhadohi asking for prices. Seventeen steps later, the carpets are on a ship and the money is in the bank.
points: Step 1, receipt of enquiry and sending quotations: the importer asks about prices, quality and terms; the exporter replies with a quotation, often in the form of a proforma invoice (giving details of quality, grade, size, weight, price and terms of export).
Step 2, receipt of order or indent: if the importer accepts, he places an order or indent describing the goods, price, quantity, packing and delivery terms.

Step 3, assessing the importer's creditworthiness and securing a guarantee for payment: the exporter usually asks for a letter of credit, a guarantee issued by the importer's bank that it will honour payment up to a certain amount.

Step 4, obtaining an export licence: the exporter must get an Importer Exporter Code (IEC) number from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), and register with the appropriate Export Promotion Council (getting a Registration-cum-Membership Certificate, RCMC); registration with the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) protects against payment risks.
Step 5, obtaining pre-shipment finance from a bank to buy raw materials, process and pack goods; Step 6, production or procurement of goods as per the importer's specifications.

example.q: Put these early export steps in order: obtain IEC number, receive order, send proforma invoice, get letter of credit.
steps: First reply to the enquiry with a proforma invoice (quotation).

Then obtain the export licence, including the IEC number.
example.answer: Send proforma invoice → receive order → get letter of credit → obtain IEC number.

topics.title: Export procedure (II): from inspection to payment

learn.hook: The carpets are ready. Now come inspection, customs, the ship's receipt, the bill of lading and finally the payment.
points: Step 7, shipment inspection: for certain goods, inspection by the Export Inspection Agency (EIA) or another authorised body is compulsory, and a certificate of inspection is issued. Step 8, excise clearance: the book lists this step, in which the exporter applies to the excise authorities for clearance of excise duty on the goods; such duty on exports was generally exempted or refunded, and since 2017 GST has replaced central excise on most goods, with exports treated as zero-rated. Step 9, obtaining a certificate of origin, which shows the country where goods are made, so the importer may claim tariff concessions.

Step 10, reservation of shipping space: the exporter applies to the shipping company; it issues a shipping order, an instruction to the captain of the ship to receive the specified goods on board. Step 11, packing and forwarding: goods are properly packed and marked and sent to the port. Step 12, insurance of goods against risks at sea.

Step 13, customs clearance: the exporter prepares a shipping bill, the main document on the basis of which customs gives permission to export. Step 14, obtaining mate's receipt: after loading, the captain (mate) of the ship issues a mate's receipt to the exporter, acknowledging receipt of the cargo on board.

Step 15, payment of freight and issue of bill of lading: on paying freight, the shipping company issues a bill of lading, which is evidence that it has accepted the goods for carriage and is a document of title (an airway bill is used for air cargo). Step 16, preparation of invoice, stating quantity and the amount payable.

Step 17, securing payment: the exporter sends the shipping documents through his bank to the importer's bank, along with a bill of exchange. Under a sight draft, documents are released on payment (D/P); under a usance draft, documents are released on acceptance of the bill (D/A), and payment is made later.

example.q: Arrange: bill of lading, shipping bill, mate's receipt, shipping order.
steps: Book space: the shipping company issues the shipping order.

On paying freight, the shipping company issues the bill of lading.
example.answer: Shipping order → shipping bill → mate's receipt → bill of lading.

learn.hook: A Ludhiana firm wants machines from Germany. It must find a supplier, get permission, arrange foreign currency, pay and clear customs before the machines reach its factory.
points: Step 1, trade enquiry: the importer collects information about exporters and their terms, and asks for quotations (often receiving a proforma invoice). Step 2, procurement of import licence: the importer checks the EXIM policy to see if a licence is needed, and must have an IEC number from the DGFT.

Step 3, obtaining foreign exchange: the importer applies to a bank authorised by the RBI for foreign exchange, as per foreign exchange regulations. Step 4, placing order or indent with the exporter. Step 5, obtaining a letter of credit from his bank in favour of the exporter, if agreed.

Step 6, arranging finance to pay for the goods on arrival. Step 7, receipt of shipment advice from the exporter, giving details such as invoice number, bill of lading number, name of vessel, port and date of shipment.

Step 8, retirement of import documents: the importer pays (sight draft) or accepts the bill of exchange (usance draft) to get the shipping documents, such as the bill of lading, from the bank. Step 9, arrival of goods at the port.

Step 10, customs clearance and release of goods: the importer gets a delivery order from the shipping company, pays the dock dues (getting a port trust dues receipt), fills in a bill of entry (giving details of goods for customs and assessment of import duty), gets the goods examined and pays the import duty; the goods are then released.

learn.hook: International trade runs on paper (or PDFs): one document orders, another guarantees payment, another proves the goods are on the ship. Mix them up and the cargo gets stuck.
points: Indent: an order placed by the importer with the exporter for supply of goods. Proforma invoice: a quotation giving details of quality, grade, size, weight, price and terms.

Letter of credit (LC): a guarantee by the importer's bank that it will honour payment up to a certain amount on presentation of specified documents. Certificate of origin: shows the country of manufacture.
Shipping order: issued by the shipping company to the ship's captain to receive the specified goods on board. Shipping bill: the main document for customs permission to export.

Mate's receipt: issued by the captain after the cargo is loaded. Bill of lading: issued by the shipping company accepting goods for carriage by sea; a document of title. Airway bill: the equivalent document for goods sent by air.

Bill of exchange: a written instrument in which the exporter (drawer) orders the importer (drawee) to pay a certain sum to a specified person. Sight draft: payable on presentation (documents released against payment). Usance draft: payable after a specified period (documents released against acceptance).

learn.hook: Which body sets rules so that 160-plus countries can trade without endless trade wars? The World Trade Organization, headquartered in Geneva.
points: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947 and effective from 1948, governed world trade for decades. The Uruguay Round of negotiations led to the creation of the World Trade Organization (WTO), which came into being on 1 January 1995 as the successor to GATT.

The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. India is a founder member. Unlike GATT, the WTO is a permanent organisation with a legal status, and it covers trade in goods, services and intellectual property.

Objectives: to raise standards of living; to ensure full employment and growth in real income and effective demand; to expand production and trade in goods and services; to ensure optimal use of the world's resources; to protect the environment and promote sustainable development; to help developing countries get a fair share of growth in world trade; and to reduce tariffs and other trade barriers and eliminate discrimination.
Note: the complexities of international business, export promotion incentives and support organisations, and export processing zones were removed in rationalisation and are not covered here.

Sustainable development is part of its aims.
The WTO aims to increase trade barriers between countries.
It aims to reduce barriers and discrimination.
GATT was the predecessor of the WTO.
The WTO replaced GATT.

items.q: Year the WTO came into being
City where the WTO is headquartered

quiz.q: The WTO came into existence on
quiz.explain: It started functioning on 1 January 1995.
steps: The WTO started functioning on 1 January 1995.
1948 is when GATT came into effect.
Answer: 1 January 1995
quiz.mistake: Confuses with GATT (1948) or Indian dates

quiz.q: The WTO is the successor of
quiz.explain: The WTO replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
steps: The Uruguay Round created the WTO to replace GATT.
So the WTO is GATT's successor.
Answer: GATT
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other international bodies

quiz.q: The headquarters of the WTO is in
quiz.explain: It is located in Geneva, Switzerland.
steps: The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.
Answer: Geneva
quiz.mistake: Confuses with UN or World Bank headquarters

quiz.q: Which is an objective of the WTO?
options: Ensuring optimal use of the world's resources
quiz.explain: Optimal resource use is a stated objective.
steps: WTO objectives include raising living standards, expanding trade and optimal use of world resources.
It seeks lower tariffs and no discrimination.
Answer: Ensuring optimal use of the world's resources

quiz.q: How does the WTO differ from GATT?
options: The WTO covers only goods, while GATT covered services
The WTO is a permanent organisation that also covers services and intellectual property
The WTO has no legal status
GATT was created after the WTO
quiz.explain: The WTO has wider scope and a permanent legal status.
steps: GATT was an agreement covering goods.
The WTO is a permanent organisation with legal status, covering goods, services and IP.
Answer: The WTO is a permanent organisation that also covers services and intellectual property

quiz.q: The WTO helps developing countries mainly by
options: working to ensure they get a fair share in the growth of world trade
quiz.explain: Special attention to developing countries is an objective.
steps: One WTO objective is to help developing countries get a fair share of growth in world trade.
Answer: working to ensure they get a fair share in the growth of world trade
quiz.mistake: Thinks the WTO restricts developing nations

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The WTO aims to reduce tariffs and other barriers to trade. Reason (R): Lower trade barriers help expand trade in goods and services among member countries.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; expanding trade is why the WTO seeks lower barriers.
steps: A: the WTO aims to reduce trade barriers – true.
R: lower barriers expand trade among members – true.
Expanding trade is the reason.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The WTO was set up in 1948. Reason (R): GATT came into effect in 1948.
options: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
quiz.explain: A is false: the WTO came into being in 1995. R is true.
steps: A: WTO set up in 1948 – false; it came in 1995.
R: GATT came into effect in 1948 – true.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true

revise.summary: The WTO, successor to GATT, came into being on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round and is based in Geneva. It is a permanent body covering goods, services and IP, aiming to expand trade, raise living standards and reduce trade barriers.
focus: How the WTO differs from GATT
remember: WTO: 1 January 1995, Geneva, successor to GATT
GATT: signed 1947, effective 1948
India is a founder member
traps: Don't say the WTO was set up in 1948; that was GATT
The WTO's headquarters is Geneva, not New York
The WTO aims to reduce, not raise, tariffs
